summary: Describes using elliptic curve cryptography in the SSH transport protocol, specifying ECDH and ECMQV key agreement and ECDSA for signatures.

plainLanguage.summary: Elliptic curve cryptography is a family of public-key methods that reach the same level of protection with much shorter keys than the older methods. This document plugs three of them into SSH: a way to sign with a curve key, a way to agree on a shared secret with a curve key, and an optional second way to agree on a shared secret.

subtitle: How SSH adopted elliptic curve key exchange and signatures: ECDH, ECMQV and ECDSA.

tldr.problem: SSH needed public-key algorithms that give strong security with small keys, and the elliptic curve family was becoming widely used.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines ecdsa-sha2-* host keys and signatures, ecdh-sha2-* key exchange and an optional ecmqv-sha2 key exchange, with named curves and SHA2 hashes chosen by curve size.
tldr.outcome: Every compliant implementation MUST support the ecdsa-sha2-* key format and ECDH key exchange on three required NIST curves. Servers that do not know the new names simply skip them during negotiation.

facts.label: Smallest curve allowed
facts.value: SHOULD NOT be smaller than 160 bits

today: RFC 5656 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the specification for using elliptic curve cryptography in the SSH transport layer. Its key exchange messages use the message numbers 30 and 31 that RFC 4250 reserves for key-exchange-specific use.

sections.title: Introduction: Elliptic Curves in SSH
sections.content:
This document adds the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) to the Secure Shell arsenal, as well as utilizing the SHA2 family of secure hash algorithms. Support is also provided for Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (ECMQV).

Due to its small key sizes and its inclusion in the National Security Agency's Suite B, Elliptic Curve Cryptography is becoming a widely utilized and attractive public-key cryptosystem. Compared to cryptosystems such as RSA, the Digital Signature Algorithm, and Diffie-Hellman key exchange, ECC variations on these schemes offer equivalent security with smaller key sizes. The table below gives approximate comparable key sizes for symmetric and asymmetric cryptosystems, based on Section 5.6.1 of NIST 800-57, which gives approximate comparable key sizes based on the best known algorithms for attacking them. L is the field size and N is the sub-field size.

The document is concerned with SSH implementation details. The specification of the underlying cryptographic algorithms is left to other standards documents, so an implementation requires familiarity with both SSH and elliptic curve cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: Elliptic curve methods reach the same level of protection as RSA or Diffie-Hellman with much shorter keys, which matters on slow links and small devices. This document says exactly how those methods plug into the SSH handshake: what the keys look like on the wire, what the messages contain, and what the two ends call each algorithm.

sections.title: The ECC Public Key Format and Signatures
sections.content:
The SSH ECC public key algorithm is defined by its key format, the corresponding signature algorithm ECDSA, the signature encoding, and the algorithm identifiers. The document defines the family of ecdsa-sha2-* public key formats and corresponding signature formats, and every compliant SSH ECC implementation MUST implement this public key format.

The ecdsa-sha2-* key formats all have the same encoding: a string ecdsa-sha2-[identifier] followed by an ecc_key_blob byte array. The blob itself contains the string [identifier], which is the identifier of the elliptic curve domain parameters, and the string Q, the public key encoded from an elliptic curve point into an octet string. Point compression MAY be used. The algorithm for ECC key generation produces a key pair containing a private key, an integer d, and a public key, an elliptic curve point Q.

Signing and verifying is done using ECDSA. The message hashing algorithm MUST be from the SHA2 family and is chosen according to the curve size. Signatures are encoded as the string ecdsa-sha2-[identifier] followed by the string ecdsa_signature_blob, which holds two integers, r and s, the output of the ECDSA algorithm. The width of the integer fields is determined by the curve being used. The integers r and s are integers modulo the order of the cryptographic subgroup, which may be larger than the size of the finite field.
sections.plainLanguage: An ECC host key is a short text name naming the curve, followed by the public point on that curve. A signature is the same name plus two numbers that a verifier checks against the message. The hash used to digest the message is picked from the SHA2 family based on how big the curve is.

sections.title: The ECDH Key Exchange
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange method generates a shared secret from an ephemeral local elliptic curve private key and an ephemeral remote elliptic curve public key. It provides explicit server authentication as defined in RFC 4253, using a signature on the exchange hash. Every compliant SSH ECC implementation MUST implement ECDH key exchange.

The primitive used for shared key generation is ECDH with cofactor multiplication. Algorithm negotiation chooses the public key algorithm used for signing and the method name of the key exchange, and the method name determines the elliptic curve domain parameters and hash function used for the rest of the exchange. All elliptic curve public keys MUST be validated after they are received; if a key fails validation, the key exchange MUST fail.

The exchange has two messages. The client sends SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT with the client's ephemeral public key octet string. The server responds with SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY carrying the server's public host key, the server's ephemeral public key octet string, and the signature on the exchange hash. The exchange hash H is the hash of the concatenation of the client's and server's identification strings, the payloads of the two SSH_MSG_KEXINIT messages, the server's public host key, the two ephemeral public key octet strings, and the shared secret K. It is RECOMMENDED that the client verify that the host key sent is the server's host key, for example using a local database; the client MAY accept the host key without verification, but doing so will render the protocol insecure against active attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends one temporary public key, the server sends one back along with its host key and a signature, and both sides compute the same shared secret from the two temporary keys. The signature over the exchange hash is what proves the server really is the server. If the client never checks that the host key is one it already trusts, an attacker in the middle can take over the connection.

sections.title: The ECMQV Key Exchange
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone key exchange algorithm generates a shared secret from two local elliptic curve key pairs and two remote public keys. It provides implicit server authentication as defined in RFC 4253, and the ECMQV key exchange method is OPTIONAL. The method name is ecmqv-sha2, which gives a hashing algorithm to be used for the HMAC. Unlike the ECDH method, ECMQV relies on a public key algorithm that uses ECC keys, so it does not need a family of method names: the curve information can be gained from the public key algorithm.

In general the ECMQV key exchange uses the ephemeral and long-term key pair of both the client and the server, which is a total of four keys. Within SSH the client does not have a long-term key pair that needs to be authenticated, so an ephemeral key is generated and used as both of the client's keys. This is more efficient than using two different ephemeral keys, and it does not adversely affect security.

During algorithm negotiation with the SSH_MSG_KEXINIT messages, ECMQV can only be chosen if a public key algorithm supporting ECC host keys can also be chosen, because it relies on implicit server authentication. If ECMQV is chosen, the public key algorithm supporting ECC host keys MUST also be chosen. ECMQV requires that all the keys used to generate a shared secret are generated over the same elliptic curve domain parameters, and because the host key is used in the generation of the shared secret, the domain parameters associated with the host key are used throughout.

The messages are SSH_MSG_ECMQV_INIT with the client's ephemeral public key octet string, and SSH_MSG_ECMQV_REPLY with the server's public host key, the server's ephemeral public key octet string, and the HMAC tag computed on the exchange hash using the shared secret. The hash is formed by applying HASH to the same list of fields as for ECDH.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an optional second way to agree on a shared secret. Instead of the server signing a hash of the exchange, both sides compute a tag over that hash using the shared secret itself, and the server's long-term key is mixed into the secret. That makes the server's identity implicit, and it means the client needs no permanent key of its own.

sections.title: Method Names and Curve Identifiers
sections.content:
The document defines a new family of key exchange method names, a new key exchange method name, and a new family of public key algorithm names in the SSH name registry. For the required curves nistp256, nistp384 and nistp521, the elliptic curve domain parameter identifiers are the strings nistp256, nistp384 and nistp521. Implementations MUST use the string identifiers for the three required NIST curves, even when an OID exists for that curve.

For all other curves, including all other NIST curves and all other recommended curves, the identifier is the ASCII period-separated decimal representation of the ASN.1 Object Identifier of the named curve domain parameters associated with the server's ECC host keys. That identifier is defined only if the concatenation of the public key format identifier and the curve identifier does not exceed the maximum specified by the SSH protocol architecture, namely 64 characters; otherwise the identifier for that curve is undefined and the curve is not supported by this specification.

The ECC public key algorithm name is the concatenation of the string ecdsa-sha2- with the curve identifier. The ECDH method name is the concatenation of ecdh-sha2- with the curve identifier. For example, the method name for ECDH key exchange with ephemeral keys generated on the sect409k1 curve is ecdh-sha2-1.3.132.0.36. The hashing algorithm from the SHA2 family is chosen based on the size of the named curve: SHA-256 for a curve of at most 256 bits, SHA-384 for a curve above 256 and at most 384 bits, and SHA-512 for a curve above 384 bits. The document contains one slip in its examples: it writes the method name for ECDH key exchange with ephemeral keys generated on the nistp256 curve as ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, using the public key algorithm prefix instead of the ecdh-sha2- prefix that Section 6.3 defines.
sections.plainLanguage: Each algorithm gets a name that states the curve it uses, so the two ends cannot disagree about which curve is in play. Three curves have short friendly names; every other curve is named by its long numeric object identifier. The hash is then fixed by the curve size, so there is no second thing to negotiate.

sections.title: Required and Recommended Curves
sections.content:
Implementations MAY support any ASN.1 object identifier in the ASN.1 object tree that defines a set of elliptic curve domain parameters. Every SSH ECC implementation MUST support the named curves nistp256, nistp384 and nistp521, which are defined in SEC 2 and were originally defined in the NIST curves document. These curves SHOULD always be enabled unless specifically disabled by local security policy.

It is RECOMMENDED that implementations also support nistk163, nistp192, nistp224, nistk233, nistb233, nistk283, nistk409, nistb409 and nistt571. For these recommended curves the identifier is the ASCII representation of the object identifier of the curve, not the NIST name.

Implementers SHOULD allow system administrators to disable some curves, including required or recommended curves, to meet local security policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Three curves are mandatory: the 256-bit, 384-bit and 521-bit NIST curves. Nine more are recommended. Administrators should still be able to switch individual curves off if their local policy demands it, even the mandatory ones.

sections.title: Impact on Network Operation
sections.content:
As the document only provides new public key algorithms and key exchange methods within the existing Secure Shell protocol architecture, there are few manageability considerations beyond those that apply to existing implementations. The Secure Shell protocol provides negotiation mechanisms for public key algorithms and key exchange methods: any implementations that do not recognize the algorithms and methods defined here will ignore them in the negotiation and use the next mutually supported algorithm or method, causing no negative impact on backward compatibility.

The use of elliptic curve cryptography should not place a significant computational burden on an implementing server. Because of its smaller key sizes, elliptic curve cryptography can be implemented more efficiently for the same security level than RSA, finite field Diffie-Hellman, or DSA.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing breaks. A server that has never heard of these names simply does not offer them, and the client picks the next algorithm both ends support. Elliptic curves are also cheap enough to run that they do not burden a server compared with RSA.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For all three classes of functionality added here, the current best known technique for breaking the cryptosystems is by solving the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. The difficulty of breaking it depends on the size and quality of the curve parameters. Certain types of curves are more susceptible to known attacks than others: for example, curves over finite fields GF(2^m) where m is composite may be susceptible to an attack based on the Weil descent, though none of the recommended curves has this problem. The required curves were all generated verifiably pseudorandomly, and the best known general attack at present is the Pollard-rho method.

An N-bit elliptic curve offers roughly the same security as an N/2-bit symmetric cipher, so the 256-bit required curve is suitable for use with 128-bit AES. Many estimates consider 2^80 to 2^90 operations to be beyond feasible, which would suggest using elliptic curves of at least 160 to 180 bits. The required curves in this document are 256-, 384- and 521-bit curves, and implementations SHOULD NOT use curves smaller than 160 bits. Not all elliptic curves are secure, even if they are over a large field, so administrators should be cautious when enabling curves other than the ones specified.

The key exchange methods rely on the SHA2 family of hash functions. Although some weaknesses have been discovered in the predecessor SHA-1, no weaknesses in the SHA2 family are known at present. Because ECDH and ECMQV allow curves of arbitrary sizes, it is important that the size of the elliptic curve be chosen to match the security strength of other elements of the SSH handshake; host key sizes, hashing algorithms and bulk encryption algorithms must be chosen appropriately. If ECDSA is used as the signature algorithm and ECDH as the key exchange method and curves of different sizes are used, then different hash functions from the SHA2 family could be used.

Implementers SHOULD ensure that any ephemeral private keys or random values, including the value k used in ECDSA signature generation and the ephemeral private key values in ECDH and ECMQV, are generated from a random number generator or a properly seeded pseudorandom number generator, are protected from leakage, are not reused outside the context of the protocol, and are erased from memory when no longer needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The strength of these methods rests on the curve, so the choice of curve matters more than usual: some curves over special fields are known to be weak, and the document lists curves that avoid that. The hash must also match the curve size, and the curve should match the strength of the rest of the handshake. One more rule is easy to get wrong: the temporary keys and the random value used in making a signature must come from a good random source and must never be reused.

data.title: ecdsa-sha2-* key format and signature encoding
data.code:
Key format:
  string   "ecdsa-sha2-[identifier]"
  byte[n]  ecc_key_blob

ecc_key_blob:
  string   [identifier]
  string   Q

Signature:
  string   "ecdsa-sha2-[identifier]"
  string   ecdsa_signature_blob

ecdsa_signature_blob:
  mpint    r
  mpint    s
